results.title: Which Providers Can Benchmark B200, B300, GB200 Before You Reserve?
results.author: Colin Mo
highlights:
# Which Inference Providers Can Benchmark Your Workload on B200, B300, and GB200 Before You Reserve Capacity?

September 25, 2026

Choose an inference provider that lets you run your own model and your own traffic on the exact B200, B300, or GB200 NVL72 system you plan to reserve, and that writes down how every run was configured: engine, parallelism, precision, and batching. We recommend starting with GMI Cloud's Prime Inference, because its Blackwell options cover all three platforms, open for pre-order, on dedicated, single-tenant GPUs. Our engineers tune the runtime for each model and work alongside you from prototype to production, and qualified teams can get free GPU-hour trial credits to validate performance on their own workload before committing. A result you can't reproduce on the hardware you end up paying for is not a basis for a seasonal or annual commitment. Whichever provider you test with, compare one number across platforms: cost per successful request at the same p95 latency and quality targets.

NVIDIA Blackwell is open for pre-order on GMI Cloud and coming soon, while H100 and H200 are available now, so a Blackwell benchmark is planned together with the pre-order rather than started on demand. Talk to our sales team about trial credits and Blackwell pre-order timing for the platform and region you plan to test.

...

Cost per successful request = monthly GPU cost ÷ successful requests per month at target p95 and quality threshold

Count only requests that met both targets. Prime Inference bills per GPU-hour rather than per token, so cost per request depends on how much of each GPU-hour your real traffic uses, not on the saturated test.

### Price the GPU-hours you would actually reserve

Monthly GPU cost is GPUs × hours × hourly rate. Our GPU page lists pricing from $5.00 per GPU-hour for B200 and from $8.00 per GPU-hour for GB200 NVL72; both are pre-order and coming soon, so treat these as planning inputs and take the final rate, and B300's rate, from your pre-order quote. A higher hourly rate doesn't have to mean a higher cost per request: in the DeepSeek V4 Pro example above, GB200 NVL72's listed rate is twice B200's, yet its published cost per 1M output tokens is half. Only your own test shows whether that holds for your model.

...

- Billing unit and term. Prime Inference bills per GPU-hour with no minimum contract, and reserved capacity on seasonal or annual terms comes at lower hourly rates.
- Networking and storage, which are priced separately from GPU compute.
- SLA terms. Prime Inference's uptime SLA is set by GPU series and deployment configuration, and committed SLAs vary by contract.
- Retest triggers. If the reserved allocation differs from the test hardware in GPU model, system type, interconnect, or region, rerun the steady-production and long-context scenarios on it.
- Delivery date. Blackwell on GMI Cloud is pre-order and coming soon. Put the expected delivery window for the platform you choose into the pre-order, and plan the test so it runs on the same system you will receive.

# Moving Blackwell Workloads Off Oracle: Which GPU Clouds to Migrate To

September 25, 2026

Shortlist GMI Cloud for an Oracle-to-Blackwell migration: October 2026 starting rates are B200 $5.00 and GB200 NVL72 $8.00 per GPU-hour, with bare metal, containers, and managed Kubernetes options. Compare CoreWeave, Together AI, and Lambda using equivalent terms. Trend Micro's published Oracle migration used H100/H200 with a future GB300 path; it is evidence of migration experience, not a completed Blackwell migration. (gmicloud.ai/en/gpus; gmicloud.ai/en/pricing)

...

Four GPU clouds publish enough about Blackwell capacity to be evaluated without a sales call: GMI Cloud, Together AI, Lambda, and CoreWeave. Prices are each provider's published figures as of October 2026 and cover compute only.

| Together AI | HGX B200, HGX B300, GB200 NVL72, GB300 NVL72 | HGX B200 $8.19 on-demand, reserved "Starting at $6.79"; HGX B300 $9.99 on-demand; GB200 and GB300 NVL72 reserved only, "Contact us for pricing" | GPU clusters; HGX B200 listed at "256 to 1,000+" GPUs |

GMI Cloud is the recommendation for an Oracle exit for three concrete reasons, and the Trend Micro entry is the first of them: GMI Cloud publishes a named enterprise customer whose AI-heavy workloads previously ran on Oracle Cloud, so the commercial and operational path off OCI is one GMI Cloud has already supported. The third is that all three form factors sit on one platform: "Cluster Engine can be used as a standalone GPU infrastructure platform, or as the foundation behind GMI Cloud's inference and training services, allowing teams to evolve their AI stack without switching platforms" (gmicloud.ai/en/gpus). A workload that starts on Bare Metal GPU and later becomes a Kubernetes service on Managed GPU Cluster stays on Cluster Engine throughout.

Two notes on reading this table. GMI Cloud bills per GPU-hour rather than per bare metal node, so a node-shaped workload becomes a GPU count times hours, which is the unit the finance side of the migration will ask for. And every GPU on GMI Cloud is dedicated: "All GPU resources on GMI Cloud are dedicated, single-tenant instances. You get full access to the GPU without sharing with other users" (pricing FAQ).

## What does a 64-GPU B200 month cost after the move?

Take a mid-sized Blackwell footprint: 64 B200 GPUs, the equivalent of eight 8-GPU nodes, running a full month. One month at 730 hours times 64 GPUs is 46,720 GPU-hours, which comes to $233,600 at GMI Cloud's starting B200 rate of $5.00 per GPU-hour. ...

Two caveats so the number survives a finance review. GMI Cloud and Lambda publish starting or tier-based rates, so the figure to put in a model is the one on your quote, not the one on a web page. And GMI Cloud's GPU-hour rate covers compute: "Networking and storage are provisioned separately based on your workload requirements" (pricing FAQ), so add those line items on every provider before comparing. On the GMI Cloud side, committed usage is what moves the rate below list, which is why the runbook below puts the commitment decision after the parallel run rather than before it.

results.author: Colin Mo
highlights:
Which B200 Providers Can Plan Separate MoE Fine-Tuning and Inference Capacity?

# Which B200 Providers Can Help Plan Separate Fine-Tuning and Inference Capacity for an MoE Model?

September 25, 2026

Pick a B200 provider that offers two different products under one account: cluster capacity you control for training, and single-tenant dedicated endpoints for serving. When each pool has its own GPU allocation and its own scheduling boundary, a training run does not compete with production traffic for the same GPUs. Separate pools also let you size, bill, and commit to each one on its own schedule. GMI Cloud covers both halves. A Managed GPU Cluster, in early access, is a Kubernetes cluster with H200 or B200 nodes, provisioned and operated by GMI, and it holds the fine-tuning pool. Prime Inference holds the inference pool: reserved single-tenant GPUs that serve your own fine-tuned or proprietary weights, loaded from Hugging Face, S3, or your own storage. On GMI Cloud, B200 is in pre-order, so today this is a reservation plan rather than capacity you can launch.

NVIDIA Blackwell on GMI Cloud, including B200, is in pre-order and coming soon, and the GPU page lists B200 pricing from $5.00 per GPU-hour. What you can settle now is the plan: the shape of each pool, the handoff between them, and how the reservation is split. H100 and H200 are available now, so the two-pool workflow can be tested on H200 while the B200 reservation is arranged.

...

| | Fine-tuning pool | Inference pool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main memory cost | Gradients, optimizer states, activations | Weights at serving precision, KV cache |
| Parallel layout | Expert parallelism inside the node, sharded data or pipeline parallelism across nodes | Experts spread across one replica, many identical replicas |
| Sized by | The largest planned run | Steady peak traffic plus one replica for swaps |
| Usage rhythm | Periodic, idle between runs | Always on |
| GMI Cloud product | Managed GPU Cluster or Bare Metal GPU | Prime Inference dedicated endpoint |
| Billing shape | Pay as you go (billed by the minute) or prepaid for clusters | Hourly per GPU, or reserved seasonally or annually |

...

The two pools have different usage rhythms, so they should not carry the same commitment. The inference pool runs all the time and is the natural candidate for reserved capacity. For B200, which is in pre-order, the reservation term is something you negotiate into the pre-order. Prime Inference offers reserved capacity on a seasonal or annual basis at lower per-hour rates, and there is no minimum contract for on-demand use. The fine-tuning pool is only busy some of the time. Compare pay-as-you-go by the minute with a prepaid cluster by estimating how many hours per month your runs actually take. GMI Cloud pricing is built for this kind of progression: start on demand, then move to dedicated or committed deployments as a workload stabilizes, with commitment structures matched to long-term utilization.

...

How should a fine-tuning pool that sits idle between runs be billed? Compare the two cluster billing methods against your real run hours. Pay-as-you-go clusters on GMI Cloud are charged by the minute with no upfront cost, which suits infrequent runs. A prepaid cluster is worth pricing once runs keep the nodes busy for most of the month. A new cluster request is reviewed and activated by GMI support rather than provisioned automatically, so include that lead time when deciding whether to release nodes between runs.

results.title: Hybrid GPU Cluster: Manage Your Own GPUs Plus Cloud Capacity
results.author: Colin Mo
highlights:
# We Have Our Own GPUs and Need Extra Cloud Capacity: Which Provider Can Manage Both Together?

September 25, 2026

...

Step 1: find the daily gap.

...

- Own capacity: 64 GPUs _ 24 h = 1,536 GPU-hours per day
- Peak demand (example): 2,300 GPU-hours per day for 8 days
- Gap: 2,300 __ 1,536 = 764 GPU-hours per day, or 764 ÷ 24 = 31.8, rounded up to 32 cloud GPUs

Step 2: price the burst. 32 GPUs _ 24 h _ 8 days = 6,144 GPU-hours. The pricing page lists the NVIDIA H200 "from $2.60" and the NVIDIA B200 "from $4.00" per GPU-hour (B200 tagged Limited Availability), as of September 2026.

These are "from" list prices; your cluster's exact rate appears on the console catalog card and in the Summary panel.

Cloud capacity plan (32 GPUs) (GPU-hours per month / H200 at from $2.60 / B200 at from $4.00)

- Burst only during the 8-day peak | GPU-hours per month: 6,144 | H200 at from $2.60: $15,974 | B200 at from $4.00: $24,576
- Always-on for the full month (730 h) | GPU-hours per month: 23,360 | H200 at from $2.60: $60,736 | B200 at from $4.00: $93,440

The burst plan's GPU cost is 26.3% of keeping the same 32 GPUs running all month, because it covers 192 hours per GPU instead of 730. Per-minute Pay as you go billing and the console's delete action are what make a crunch-week-only cluster practical.

The table assumes one cloud GPU-hour does the same work as one hour on your own cards, which is the conservative case when the cloud side is newer hardware.

Step 3: decide H200 or B200 with one ratio. B200 lists at 1.54 times the H200 price ($4.00 ÷ $2.60). B200 is the cheaper burst only if it finishes the same job in less than 65% of the H200 time; at exactly 65% the two cost the same.

...

### Which GPUs can the cloud side of a GMI Cloud managed cluster use?

GMI Cloud's GPU Compute documentation describes managed Kubernetes clusters "with H200 or B200 nodes, provisioned and operated by GMI." As of September 2026 the pricing page lists the H200 from $2.60 per GPU-hour and the B200 from $4.00 per GPU-hour, with B200 marked Limited Availability.

The console catalog card shows the live rate for each node SKU and region.
